The greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in cranial dimensions, with adult females attaining a maximum head length of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters], whereas adult males achieve a substantially larger ultimate head length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters]. This size disparity is closely linked to the species' polygynous mating system, where larger males likely benefit from enhanced competitive abilities during encounters with rivals. Neonatal offspring emerge following a brief gestation period, with the wet weight at birth recorded at just 0.245 grams [Wwb = 0.245 grams]. This remarkably diminutive birth mass, typical of marsupials, necessitates an extended period of dependency within the maternal pouch, where the altricial neonate undergoes most of its early morphological development while continuously suckling.

Reproductive output in the greater bilby is remarkably high for a medium-sized marsupial when evaluated under optimal thermal conditions. At a stable environmental temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], females achieve their maximum reproductive rate by producing two pups per litter [N_R_i = two pups per litter] and successfully rearing up to four litters per year [F_R_i = up to four litters per year]. This high fecundity is an adaptation to the variable and often harsh arid environments the species inhabits, where juvenile survivorship can be low. The short gestation, coupled with the ability to rapidly produce successive litters when food resources are abundant following unpredictable rainfall events, allows populations to rebound quickly after periods of drought-induced decline. The timing of these litters is therefore closely synchronized with resource pulses.

Under controlled captive conditions maintained at a body temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], the gestation period for Macrotis lagotis is precisely 17 days [tg = 17 days]. This exceptionally brief uterine development is characteristic of many marsupials and reflects the energetic expediency of giving birth to an underdeveloped neonate that completes its growth externally while nursing. Following parturition, the altricial young remain continuously attached to a teat within the pouch, progressing through a critical phase of suckling dependency. The time since birth at weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence from milk, occurs at 110 days [tx = 110 days] at this same stable temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This extended period of lactation support is vital for the offspring's immune system development and acquisition of foraging skills.

Sexual maturation in the greater bilby is attained several weeks after weaning, signifying the onset of gametogenesis and the capacity to enter the breeding population. The time since birth at puberty has been recorded at 150 days [tp = 150 days] under captive conditions maintained at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This relatively rapid progression to reproductive competence, occurring roughly five months after birth, represents a fast life-history strategy that enables young-of-the-year to contribute to the breeding population within their first season. The ultimate wet weight for females at this adult stage typically reaches approximately 1000 grams [Wwi = approximately 1000 grams], while the ultimate wet weight for adult males, reflecting their larger body frame and head size, stabilizes around 2000 grams [Wwi = around 2000 grams]. This twofold difference in adult body mass underscores the high degree of sexual size dimorphism observed in the species.

Longevity records for the greater bilby indicate a maximum lifespan of roughly nine and a half years (roughly 9.5 years) [am = roughly 9.5 years] when calculated from field and captive data at a standard physiological temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan for a small-to-medium-sized marsupial is consistent with its low extrinsic mortality rate in protected populations, where predation pressure is reduced. Comparative analysis with other peramelemorphians reveals that Macrotis lagotis possesses a slower pace of life than many of its close relatives, likely an evolutionary response to the unpredictable resource availability of its desert habitat. The wet weight at birth of the neonate of just 0.245 grams [Wwb = 0.245 grams] stands in stark contrast to the mother's own adult mass, emphasizing the extreme altriciality and the high energetic investment required during the subsequent lactation phase to bridge that vast size gap.
